L0@P0: The UCONABC Usage Control Model
L1@P0: JAEHONG PARK
L2@P0: George Mason University
L3@P0: and
L4@P0: RAVI SANDHU
L5@P0: NSD Security and George Mason University
L6@P0: In this paper, we introduce the family of UCONABC models for usage control (UCON), which integrate Authorizations (A), oBligations (B), and Conditions (C). We call these core models because
L7@P0: they address the essence of UCON, leaving administration, delegation, and other important but
L8@P0: second-order issues for later work. The term usage control is a generalization of access control
L9@P0: to cover authorizations, obligations, conditions, continuity (ongoing controls), and mutability. Traditionally, access control has dealt only with authorization decisions on users’ access to target
L10@P0: resources. Obligations are requirements that have to be fulfilled by obligation subjects for allowing
L11@P0: access. Conditions are subject and object independent environmental or system requirements that
L12@P0: have to be satisfied for access. In today’s highly dynamic, distributed environment, obligations and
L13@P0: conditions are also crucial decision factors for richer and finer controls on usage of digital resources.
L14@P0: Although they have been discussed occasionally in recent literature, most authors have been motivated from specific target problems and thereby limited in their approaches. The UCONABC
L15@P0: model integrates these diverse concepts in a unified framework. Traditional authorization decisions are generally made at the time of requests but hardly recognize ongoing controls for relatively
L16@P0: long-lived access or for immediate revocation. Moreover, mutability issues that deal with updates
L17@P0: on related subject or object attributes as a consequence of access have not been systematically
L18@P0: studied.
L19@P0: Unlike other studies that have targeted on specific problems or issues, the UCONABC model
L20@P0: seeks to enrich and refine the access control discipline in its definition and scope. UCONABC
L21@P0: covers traditional access controls such as mandatory, discretionary, and role-based access control.
L22@P0: Digital rights management and other modern access controls are also covered. UCONABC lays the
L23@P0: foundation for next generation access controls that are required for today’s real-world information
L24@P0: and systems security. This paper articulates the core of this new area of UCON and develops several
L25@P0: detailed models.

L842: ## 2.12 Actions performed in conjunction with enforcement
L843: In many applications, policies specify actions that MUST be performed, either instead of, or in addition to, actions that MAY be performed.  This idea was described by Sloman [Sloman94].  XACML provides facilities to specify actions that MUST be performed in conjunction with policy evaluation in the <Obligations> element.  This idea was described as a provisional action by Kudo [Kudo00].  There are no standard definitions for these actions in version 3.0 of XACML.  Therefore, bilateral agreement between a PAP and the PEP that will enforce its policies is required for correct interpretation.  PEPs that conform to v3.0 of XACML are required to deny access unless they understand and can discharge all of the <Obligations> elements associated with the applicable policy.  <Obligations> elements are returned to the PEP for enforcement.
L844: ## 2.13 Supplemental information about a decision
L845: 
L846: In some applications it is helpful to specify supplemental information about a decision. XACML provides facilities to specify supplemental information about a decision with the <Advice> element. Such advice may be safely ignored by the PEP.

L848: # 3      Models (non-normative)
L849: 
L850: The data-flow model and language model of XACML are described in the following sub-sections.
L851: ## 3.1 Data-flow model
L852: 
L853: The major actors in the XACML domain are shown in the data-flow diagram of Figure 1.

L858: Note: some of the data-flows shown in the diagram may be facilitated by a repository.  For instance, the communications between the context handler and the PIP or the communications between the PDP and the PAP may be facilitated by a repository.  The XACML specification is not intended to place restrictions on the location of any such repository, or indeed to prescribe a particular communication protocol for any of the data-flows.

L860: The model operates by the following steps.
L861:   1. PAPs write policies and policy sets and make them available to the PDP.  These policies or policy sets represent the complete policy for a specified target.
L862:   2. The access requester sends a request for access to the PEP.
L863:   3. The PEP sends the request for access to the context handler in its native request format, optionally including attributes of the subjects, resource, action, environment and other categories.

L4477: ## 7.2 Policy enforcement point
L4478: 
L4479: This section describes the requirements for the PEP.
L4480: 
L4481: An application functions in the role of the PEP if it guards access to a set of resources and asks the PDP for an authorization decision. The PEP MUST abide by the authorization decision as described in one of the following sub-sections
L4482: 
L4483: In any case any advice in the decision may be safely ignored by the PEP.
L4484: ### 7.2.1 Base PEP
L4485: 
L4486: If the decision is "Permit", then the PEP SHALL permit access.  If obligations accompany the decision, then the PEP SHALL permit access only if it understands and it can and will discharge those obligations.
L4487: 
L4488: If the decision is "Deny", then the PEP SHALL deny access.  If obligations accompany the decision, then the PEP shall deny access only if it understands, and it can and will discharge those obligations.
L4489: 
L4490: If the decision is “Not Applicable”, then the PEP’s behavior is undefined.
L4491: If the decision is “Indeterminate”, then the PEP’s behavior is undefined.
L4492: ### 7.2.2 Deny-biased PEP
L4493: 
L4494: If the decision is "Permit", then the PEP SHALL permit access.  If obligations accompany the decision, then the PEP SHALL permit access only if it understands and it can and will discharge those obligations.
L4495: 
L4496: All other decisions SHALL result in the denial of access.
L4497: 
L4498: Note: other actions, e.g. consultation of additional PDPs, reformulation/resubmission of the decision request, etc., are not prohibited.
L4499: ### 7.2.3 Permit-biased PEP
L4500: 
L4501: If the decision is "Deny", then the PEP SHALL deny access.  If obligations accompany the decision, then the PEP shall deny access only if it understands, and it can and will discharge those obligations.
L4502: 
L4503: All other decisions SHALL result in the permission of access.
L4504: 
L4505: Note: other actions, e.g. consultation of additional PDPs, reformulation/resubmission of the decision request, etc., are not prohibited.
L4506: ## 7.3 Attribute evaluation
L4507: 
L4508: Attributes are represented in the request context by the context handler, regardless of whether or not they appeared in the original decision request, and are referred to in the policy by attribute designators and attribute selectors.  A named attribute is the term used for the criteria that the specific attribute designators use to refer to particular attributes in the <Attributes> elements of the request context.
L4509: ### 7.3.1 Structured attributes
L4510: 
L4511: <AttributeValue> elements MAY contain an instance of a structured XML data-type, for example <ds:KeyInfo>.  XACML 3.0 supports several ways for comparing the contents of such elements.
L4512:   1. In some cases, such elements MAY be compared using one of the XACML string functions, such as “string-regexp-match”, described below.  This requires that the element be given the data-type "http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#string".  For example, a structured data-type that is actually a ds:KeyInfo/KeyName would appear in the Context as:
L4513: 
L4514: <AttributeValue DataType="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#string">
L4515: 
L4516:    <ds:KeyName>jhibbert-key</ds:KeyName>
L4517: 
L4518: </AttributeValue>
L4519: In general, this method will not be adequate unless the structured data-type is quite simple.
L4520:   2. The structured attribute MAY be made available in the <Content> element of the appropriate attribute category and an <AttributeSelector> element MAY be used to select the contents of a leaf sub-element of the structured data-type by means of an XPath expression.  That value MAY then be compared using one of the supported XACML functions appropriate for its primitive data-type.  This method requires support by the PDP for the optional XPath expressions feature.
L4917: If "NotApplicable" is to be treated as "Permit", it is vital that the matching algorithms used by the policy to match elements in the decision request be closely aligned with the data syntax used by the applications that will be submitting the decision request.  A failure to match will result in “NotApplicable” and be treated as "Permit".  So an unintended failure to match may allow unintended access.
L4918: Commercial http responders allow a variety of syntaxes to be treated equivalently.  The "%" can be used to represent characters by hex value.  The URL path "/../" provides multiple ways of specifying the same value.  Multiple character sets may be permitted and, in some cases, the same printed character can be represented by different binary values.  Unless the matching algorithm used by the policy is sophisticated enough to catch these variations, unintended access may be permitted.
L4919: It may be safe to treat "NotApplicable" as "Permit" only in a closed environment where all applications that formulate a decision request can be guaranteed to use the exact syntax expected by the policies.  In a more open environment, where decision requests may be received from applications that use any legal syntax, it is strongly recommended that "NotApplicable" NOT be treated as "Permit" unless matching rules have been very carefully designed to match all possible applicable inputs, regardless of syntax or type variations.  Note, however, that according to Section 7.2, a PEP must deny access unless it receives an explicit “Permit” authorization decision.
L4920: ### 9.1.7 Negative rules
L4921: 
L4922: A negative rule is one that is based on a predicate not being "True".  If not used with care, negative rules can lead to policy violations, therefore some authorities recommend that they not be used.  However, negative rules can be extremely efficient in certain cases, so XACML has chosen to include them.  Nevertheless, it is recommended that they be used with care and avoided if possible.
L4923: A common use for negative rules is to deny access to an individual or subgroup when their membership in a larger group would otherwise permit them access.  For example, we might want to write a rule that allows all vice presidents to see the unpublished financial data, except for Joe, who is only a ceremonial vice president and can be indiscreet in his communications.  If we have complete control over the administration of subject attributes, a superior approach would be to define “Vice President” and “Ceremonial Vice President” as distinct groups and then define rules accordingly.  However, in some environments this approach may not be feasible.  (It is worth noting in passing that referring to individuals in rules does not scale well.  Generally, shared attributes are preferred.)
L4924: If not used with care, negative rules can lead to policy violations in two common cases:  when attributes are suppressed and when the base group changes.  An example of suppressed attributes would be if we have a policy that access should be permitted, unless the subject is a credit risk.  If it is possible that the attribute of being a credit risk may be unknown to the PDP for some reason, then unauthorized access may result.  In some environments, the subject may be able to suppress the publication of attributes by the application of privacy controls, or the server or repository that contains the information may be unavailable for accidental or intentional reasons.
L4925: An example of a changing base group would be if there is a policy that everyone in the engineering department may change software source code, except for secretaries.  Suppose now that the department was to merge with another engineering department and the intent is to maintain the same policy.  However, the new department also includes individuals identified as administrative assistants, who ought to be treated in the same way as secretaries.  Unless the policy is altered, they will unintentionally be permitted to change software source code.  Problems of this type are easy to avoid when one individual administers all policies, but when administration is distributed, as XACML allows, this type of situation must be explicitly guarded against.
L4926: ### 9.1.8 Denial of service
L4927: 
L4928: A denial of service attack is one in which the adversary overloads an XACML actor with excessive computations or network traffic such that legitimate users cannot access the services provided by the actor.

L1415@P37: 6.2 Administrative Issues in UCON
L1416@P37: In the UCONABC model, we have mainly focused on usages of consumer subjects
L1417@P37: on objects. In this section we assume that usage rules such as authorization,
L1418@P37: obligation, and condition rules are already provided. As mentioned earlier, in
L1419@P37: UCON, subjects can be either consumers, providers, or identifiees. Each subject
L1420@P37: party has close relationships with other parties. One party may influence other
L1421@P37: parties’ usage decisions. Each party holds its own rights on objects. Exercising
L1422@P37: rights on an object may require certain obligations that have to be fulfilled before, during or after the rights are exercised. Fulfillment of these obligations
L1423@P37: may create other objects (called derivative objects) that have to be protected.
L1424@P37: This series of relationships has to be resolved seamlessly in UCON as an administrative issue. Here, we discuss some fundamental issues of UCON administration briefly. We believe that the further work on administrative UCON is
L1425@P37: crucial for the success of UCON.

L1427@P37: a supply chain. If allowed by a provider, a consumer can hand over the object
L1428@P37: to another consumer and can control usage of the new consumer. In this case,
L1429@P37: the original consumer becomes a provider of the object to the new consumer.

L1624@P44: 8. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
L1625@P44: In this paper, we have introduced a novel concept called usage control and
L1626@P44: its core model called UCONABC for controlling access to and usage of digital
L1627@P44: resources. UCON encompasses traditional access control, trust management,
L1628@P44: and DRM and goes beyond them in its scope. By unifying these diverse areas
L1629@P44: in a systematic manner, the UCONABC model offers a promising approach for
L1630@P44: the next generation of access control.
